A reproducible technical note

U-Nets, from first principles to weak-lensing mass maps

What a U-Net actually is — and how the same architecture is used across modern cosmology, built up to a worked Euclid / LSST-style example trained from scratch in this note.
Dr. Dipak Munshi  ·  Advanced Research Fellow, Imperial College London  ·  part of the ML & Stat Notes series  ·  every figure generated by the code described here
deep learningU-Net weak lensingmass mapping EuclidLSST inverse problems

The U-Net is probably the single most reused neural-network design in scientific imaging. It was introduced in 2015 for segmenting biomedical microscopy [1], and the same shape now turns up everywhere a problem can be posed as "image in, image out" — including a surprising amount of cosmology. This note builds it up from nothing: what the architecture is and why it is shaped the way it is, how it moves from segmentation to regression, and then a concrete, fully reproducible weak-lensing example — recovering a dark-matter map from noisy shear — where a small U-Net, trained from scratch here, beats the classical optimal linear filter. It closes with how the architecture is used at survey scale for Euclid and LSST, and an honest account of where it can mislead you.

1The problem a U-Net solves

Dense prediction: one value (or vector) for every pixel.

An ordinary image classifier turns a whole picture into a single label — cat, galaxy, not-a-galaxy. Many scientific problems are not like that. We want an output that is itself an image, the same size as the input, with a prediction at every pixel: a cleaned-up version of a noisy map, a per-pixel class, a physical field inferred from data. This is called dense prediction, and it has two competing demands:

Context
to know what a pixel is, you need to look at a wide neighbourhood — large-scale structure, the shape of an extended source.
Localisation
but the answer must be placed back at exactly the right pixel, with fine detail preserved — a sharp peak must stay sharp and in the right spot.

These pull in opposite directions. Pooling/downsampling gives you context cheaply but throws away precise location; keeping full resolution everywhere preserves location but is blind to large-scale context and ruinously expensive. The U-Net's whole design is a clean answer to this tension.

2The architecture

A contracting path, an expanding path, and skip connections between them.

First, the four building blocks

If you have seen a neural network but not a convolutional one, four pieces are all you need:

Convolution
a small filter (say 3×3 weights) slid across the image; at each position it takes a weighted sum of the pixels under it. The same weights are reused everywhere, so the network learns one local pattern — an edge, a blob — with only nine numbers, and can find it anywhere in the image. This weight-sharing is why CNNs need far fewer parameters than a fully-connected net, and why they respect the fact that a peak is a peak wherever it sits.
Channels / feature maps
one filter produces one output image (a "feature map") highlighting where its pattern occurs. A layer runs many filters in parallel, so the single-channel input becomes a stack of, say, 16 feature maps — 16 different learned patterns. Deeper layers combine these into more abstract ones (edges → textures → objects). "c=16" in the code below just sets how many feature maps the first layer makes.
ReLU
after each convolution, replace negatives with zero (). Without a nonlinearity like this, stacking layers would collapse into one big linear filter — no more powerful than the Wiener filter in §4. ReLU is what lets the network learn a genuinely nonlinear map.
Pooling & receptive field
pooling shrinks the image (e.g. keep the max of each 2×2 block). After it, one pixel of the next layer summarises a 2×2 region of the previous one — and after several poolings, a single deep unit "sees" a large patch of the original image. That reach is its receptive field, and a large one is what lets the network use context (the surrounding structure) to decide what a pixel should be.

A U-Net is just these four blocks arranged into a particular shape. Reading it left to right:

Contracting path
the encoder. A stack of conv → ReLU → conv → ReLU → pool blocks. Each pool halves the height and width, so the receptive field of each feature grows quickly — by the bottleneck, a single unit "sees" a large patch of the input. This is the context half.
Bottleneck
the lowest-resolution, most abstract representation: what is in this image, broadly, and where things are, coarsely.
Expanding path
the decoder. Mirror image: upsample, then convolve, back up to the original resolution. This is the localisation half — it rebuilds a full-resolution output from the abstract summary.
Skip connections
the defining trick. At each level the decoder is given not just the upsampled coarse features but also the original full-resolution features from the matching encoder level, concatenated together. The network no longer has to squeeze every fine detail through the bottleneck; sharp edges and small peaks travel the short way across.

Why the skip connections matter so much

Without them, everything the output needs must survive the trip down to the bottleneck and back — and downsampling is lossy, so fine structure is blurred. The skip connections give the decoder a direct line to crisp, high-resolution information. In practice they are the difference between a plausible-but-smudged map and one with correct edges and point sources. They also give gradients a short path during training, which makes deep U-Nets stable to optimise.

A minimal but complete U-Net is remarkably short — this is essentially the network trained later in this note:

class UNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, c=16):
        # cbr = conv-relu-conv-relu block
        self.e1, self.e2, self.e3 = cbr(1,c), cbr(c,2*c), cbr(2*c,4*c)   # encoder
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.up   = nn.Upsample(scale_factor=2, mode="bilinear")
        self.d2, self.d1 = cbr(4*c+2*c, 2*c), cbr(2*c+c, c)             # decoder
        self.out  = nn.Conv2d(c, 1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        a = self.e1(x)                        # full res
        b = self.e2(self.pool(a))             # 1/2
        c = self.e3(self.pool(b))             # 1/4  (bottleneck)
        d = self.d2(torch.cat([self.up(c), b], 1))   # up + skip from b
        e = self.d1(torch.cat([self.up(d), a], 1))   # up + skip from a
        return self.out(e)                  # image out, same size as in

The two torch.cat lines are the skip connections: the encoder feature (b, a) is glued onto the upsampled decoder feature before the next block.

3From segmentation to regression

Change the last layer and the loss, and "label every pixel" becomes "predict a physical value at every pixel".

The original U-Net did segmentation: each output pixel carried a class probability (cell / not-cell), trained with a cross-entropy loss. Nothing about the body of the network cares whether the target is a class or a number. Swap the final layer for a single linear channel and train against a continuous target with a mean-squared-error loss, and the identical architecture performs image-to-image regression:

TaskOutput layerLossExample
Segmentationsoftmax over classescross-entropy / Dice galaxy vs. sky; cluster membership
Regressionlinear (1 channel)MSE / L1 denoising; recovering a physical field
Density / countssoftplus / Poisson headPoisson NLL source counts, photon maps

That one change is what makes the U-Net relevant to physics. The map we want in cosmology — the dark-matter convergence field, a denoised temperature map, a super-resolved simulation — is a continuous field, so we are almost always in the regression column. The next section makes this concrete.

4Worked example: weak-lensing mass mapping

Recovering the dark-matter map from noisy shear — the canonical cosmological inverse problem, trained from scratch in this note.

The physics in three lines

Light from distant galaxies is deflected by the gravity of the intervening matter. This weak gravitational lensing slightly distorts the observed shapes of galaxies — a coherent stretching called the shear . What we actually want is the convergence : the projected total (mostly dark) matter density. Shear and convergence are two views of the same lensing potential, linked in Fourier space by a simple operator [2]:

Because , inverting it is trivial in principle — multiply by . That is the classic Kaiser–Squires (KS) inversion. The catch is noise: each galaxy has a large random intrinsic ellipticity ("shape noise"), so the measured shear is the true signal plus a big noise term. Inverting noisy shear with KS gives an extremely noisy map. Recovering a clean from it is a genuine, ill-posed denoising / inverse problem — exactly the kind of dense-prediction task §1 described.

The ladder of methods — from naive to learned

Mass mapping is an old problem, so there is a whole ladder of ways to attack it. I implemented the lot, from the crudest to the U-Net, so the network's gain is measured against real competition, not a straw man. Each rung adds one idea:

1. Noisy KS
apply to the noisy shear — the exact inversion. Unbiased, but it passes all the shape noise straight through, so the map is swamped. This is the input every method below starts from.
2. KS + Gaussian smoothing
blur the noisy map with a Gaussian kernel. The oldest trick there is: noise is small-scale, so smoothing kills it — but it also smears the real peaks. One knob (the kernel width), no notion of signal vs. noise.
3. Wiener filter
the optimal linear estimator. In Fourier space it weights each scale by its signal-to-noise, . Smoothing done right: it keeps scales where signal dominates and suppresses scales where noise does. Provably the best linear method — if the field is Gaussian.
4. Sparse / wavelet
the first nonlinear classical method. Expand the map in wavelets (localised blobs at many scales), then soft-threshold: keep the few large coefficients (real structure), zero the many small ones (noise). This is the idea behind the MRLens and GLIMPSE mass-mapping tools — good at preserving sharp peaks that smoothing would wash out.
5. CNN without skip connections
a learned method, and a deliberate ablation: the exact same encoder–decoder as the U-Net but with the skip connections removed, trained identically. Its only disadvantage versus the U-Net is the missing skips — so the gap between them isolates what those skips are worth.
6. U-Net
the full network of §2, skips included, trained from scratch here.

Rungs 1–4 are hand-designed and need no training; rungs 5–6 learn from examples. Reading the results across all six is more instructive than any single number.

Modelling the signal: why log-normal fields

To train and test a reconstruction method we need realistic mock convergence maps. A Gaussian random field with the right power spectrum is the easy choice — but it is wrong in a way that matters here. Gravitational collapse is nonlinear: matter piles up into dense halos and clusters, and empties out into voids. The real convergence field is therefore strongly non-Gaussian — it has a hard lower bound (, you cannot have less than empty), a long positive tail of rare bright peaks, and a skewed one-point distribution.

The standard, decades-old analytic model that captures this is the log-normal field [6]: take a Gaussian field with the desired power spectrum and apply an exponential transform,

where sets the degree of non-Gaussianity. This one line turns a symmetric Gaussian field into something with realistic peaks and a skewed PDF, while keeping a well-defined power spectrum — which is exactly why log-normal mocks are a workhorse for weak-lensing and galaxy-clustering covariance studies.

Why this choice is the whole point

Two fields with the same power spectrum are indistinguishable to any method that only uses two-point information — including the Wiener filter. Everything that separates the log-normal field from the Gaussian one lives in its higher-order statistics. So by training on log-normal mocks we set up precisely the regime where a nonlinear method (the U-Net) can beat the optimal linear one (Wiener), and where my own higher-order estimators — bispectrum, skew-spectrum, PDF and morphology — are designed to extract the extra signal. Same physics, two complementary toolkits.

The experiment

To make this a fair, honest test I simulated a dataset and ran all six methods on it, training the two networks from scratch inside this note:

Signal
1 000 convergence maps (64²) drawn from a lensing-like power spectrum and then passed through the log-normal transform above — so the target fields have the realistic, skewed, non-Gaussian PDF with bright peaks.
Data
forward-shear each map with , add shape noise, invert with KS. This noisy KS map is the common input; the clean is the target. Split 800 train / 200 held-out validation.
Networks
the 3-level encoder–decoder of §2 (c=16), once with skip connections (the U-Net) and once without (the ablation CNN), MSE loss, Adam, 45 epochs. A couple of minutes each on a laptop CPU.
Fair baselines
the classical rungs need no training; the Wiener filter is given its signal and noise power spectra measured empirically from the same simulations, and the smoothing and wavelet thresholds are tuned — so every classical method is at its best.

What "training a network" actually means — the words, from scratch

The two learned methods are fitted to the examples. If the vocabulary is new, here is the whole loop in plain terms:

Weights / parameters
the numbers inside the network (all those convolution filters). "Training" means searching for the values of these numbers that make the output match the target. This network has a few hundred thousand of them.
Loss
one number that measures how wrong the current output is. Here it is the mean squared error (MSE) — the average squared difference, pixel by pixel, between the network's map and the true . Training = making the loss small.
Gradient descent
calculus gives the direction in which to nudge every weight to reduce the loss a little; the network takes a small step that way, then recomputes. Repeat thousands of times and the loss slides downhill. (The algorithm that computes all those directions at once is back-propagation.)
Learning rate
how big each step is. Too big overshoots; too small crawls. Adam is a popular rule that adapts the step size for each weight automatically — it is what "Adam, 45 epochs" refers to.
Batch
the steps are taken on small groups of examples (here 64 at a time) rather than the whole set at once — faster and a little noisy, which helps.
Epoch
one complete pass through all the training examples. One pass is never enough — each pass nudges the weights slightly, so "45 epochs" means the network saw the whole training set 45 times, improving a little each sweep.
Validation & overfitting
we watch the loss on 200 held-out maps the network never trains on. If training loss keeps falling but validation loss rises, the network is memorising the training set rather than learning the general map — "overfitting". Here the two stay together, so it has genuinely learned the task.

The result

MethodRMSEIdea it adds
Noisy Kaiser–Squires0.636exact inversion, no denoising
KS + Gaussian smoothing0.480kill small scales (and the peaks)
Wiener filter0.435optimal linear filter
Sparse / wavelet0.523first nonlinear method; keeps peaks
CNN, no skips0.555learned, but detail lost at the bottleneck
U-Net (skips)0.376learned + fine detail preserved

Two things stand out. The U-Net cuts the error ~14% below the best possible linear filter — and it beats the identical CNN without skip connections by ~32% on the same training budget. In fact the no-skip CNN cannot even match the classical Wiener filter: the skip connections are what turn the learned method from a loser into the winner. Both results have the same root cause →

Reading the ladder — and why this is my kind of problem

Why the nonlinear methods win. On a purely Gaussian field the Wiener filter is provably optimal and nothing can beat it. The convergence field is non-Gaussian, though: its peaks and skewed PDF carry information no linear filter can touch, because the optimal estimator for a non-Gaussian field is nonlinear. That is why the wavelet method and the networks pull ahead — they can treat a bright peak differently from a noisy ripple.

Why the skips matter. The CNN and the U-Net are identical except for the skip connections, yet the U-Net wins clearly — you can see it in the maps, where the no-skip CNN is visibly blurred. Without skips, every fine detail must squeeze through the low-resolution bottleneck and is smeared on the way back up; the skips hand that detail directly to the decoder. They also give gradients a short path, so the U-Net trains faster and more stably: in the curve the skip-free CNN is still crawling downhill when the U-Net has long plateaued. The gap between those two bars is the clearest possible illustration of the single idea from §2.

The cosmology connection. This is exactly the physics behind DeepMass [3] — which is itself a U-Net, and was the first deep-learning mass map applied to real survey data (DES), beating Wiener filtering on these same grounds. It is also the thread running through my own research — the weak-lensing bispectrum, skew-spectrum, convergence-map morphology and phase statistics are all ways of characterising precisely the non-Gaussian structure these methods exploit.

The classical-statistics and the deep-learning views are two routes into the same information.

(So when the applications table cites DeepMass for "mass mapping", it means mass mapping done with a U-Net — the same architecture trained here, scaled up to a real survey.)

"No skips" from first principles — and why it is really about wavelets

What "no skips" is. Strip the skip connections and you are left with a pure encoder–decoder: the image is squeezed down to the small bottleneck, and then the output is rebuilt from that bottleneck alone. Everything the network wants to say about the map has to pass through that narrow middle. This is an information bottleneck: it is lossy compression followed by decompression — like writing a one-paragraph description of a photograph and then asking someone to redraw it. You recover the gist (where the big blobs are) but not the sharp edges or the exact peak positions, because those never fit through the paragraph. That is precisely why the no-skip CNN produces a blurred map and loses to the U-Net.

The wavelet connection. This is not a loose analogy — it is almost exactly a wavelet transform. A wavelet decomposition splits an image into a coarse approximation (a blurred, downsampled version) plus a set of detail coefficients at each scale (the sharp edges and small features the blurring threw away). Crucially, it keeps those detail bands, and uses them to rebuild the image exactly. Now line the two up:

encoder downsampling
= computing the coarse, blurred approximations (the wavelet low-pass, scale by scale)
the bottleneck
= the coarsest approximation — the smallest, blurriest summary
skip connections
= the detail coefficients: the fine-scale information carried around the bottleneck and handed back at reconstruction

So a U-Net is, almost literally, a learned, nonlinear multi-resolution (wavelet-like) analysis. A no-skip autoencoder is what you get if you keep only the coarse wavelet approximation and throw away every detail band — you can only ever reconstruct a smooth, blurred image. The §4 wavelet method keeps those detail bands by hand (with a fixed transform and a threshold); the U-Net learns its own detail bands, tuned to this data — which is why it does the same job, but better. The skip connections are the U-Net's detail coefficients.

5The same architecture across cosmology

Once you see "image in, image out", U-Nets appear all over the Euclid / LSST pipeline.

Mass mapping is one instance of a pattern. The identical design — sometimes with 3D convolutions, attention, or a diffusion wrapper — is used for:

Each citation above points to a representative deep-learning paper for that application; see the References.

The common thread: these are all inverse problems on fields. Wherever cosmology has a forward model (physics → data) that is expensive or noisy to invert, a U-Net trained on simulations can learn the inverse map and run in milliseconds — which is what makes it viable at the scale of billions of Euclid and LSST galaxies. A few of these are worth a closer look.

Spotlight: four examples in a little more depth

Cosmic-web classification — U-Nets doing their original job. The large-scale structure of the universe is a "cosmic web": underdense voids, sheet-like walls, one-dimensional filaments, and dense nodes (clusters) where filaments meet. Deciding which category each point of a density field belongs to is a textbook segmentation problem — exactly what the U-Net was invented for in biology, with "cell vs. background" swapped for "filament vs. void". The network takes the 3D density field and outputs a label for every voxel, capturing the connected, multi-scale geometry that hand-tuned classifiers struggle with.

CMB component separation and delensing. The microwave sky is the primordial CMB plus Galactic dust, synchrotron, point sources and more, all mixed together across observing frequencies. Component separation is the problem of unmixing them to recover the clean CMB — a per-pixel regression from a stack of frequency maps to one output map, a natural fit for a multi-channel U-Net. A related task is delensing: gravitational lensing smears the CMB's acoustic peaks and contaminates the primordial -mode signal that probes inflation; a U-Net can learn to partially undo that smearing given a tracer of the lensing matter.

Baryon painting — cheap physics from expensive physics. Full hydrodynamic simulations (gas, stars, feedback, X-ray emission) are enormously expensive; gravity-only N-body simulations are far cheaper but lack the baryons. A U-Net can be trained to "paint" the baryonic fields onto a dark-matter-only simulation — learning the map from the dark-matter distribution to the gas, stellar and X-ray fields that a full hydro run would have produced. It is the same image-to-image idea as super-resolution, but adding physics rather than resolution.

Strong-lens finding. Strong gravitational lenses — where a foreground mass bends a background galaxy into arcs or rings — are rare and scientifically precious, and Euclid and LSST will image billions of objects. Searching by eye is impossible. Here the U-Net (or a CNN classifier built on one) scans cutouts to flag candidate lenses, and a regression U-Net can even produce a first pass at the lens mass or the de-lensed source — triaging billions of images down to a human-reviewable shortlist.

From a map to a number, with error bars

For parameter estimation, a U-Net rarely works alone. A common modern pattern is: U-Net (or similar CNN) compresses the field into a low-dimensional learned summary, and then simulation-based inference (SBI) — e.g. a normalizing flow — turns that summary into a posterior on without ever writing down a likelihood. This is the field-level inference approach now being developed for Stage-IV surveys, and it connects directly to the Bayesian-inference methods in my companion toolkit note.

6Uncertainty — and caveats and limitations

A point-estimate map is not science until it has error bars and a calibration check.

A plain U-Net gives a single "best" map with no uncertainty, which is dangerous for inference. Three standard ways to get uncertainty out of one:

MC-dropout
leave dropout on at test time, run many forward passes, take the spread — a cheap approximate-Bayesian posterior.
Deep ensembles
train several U-Nets from different seeds; their disagreement is an uncertainty estimate, often better-calibrated than dropout.
Bayesian / generative U-Nets
output a full posterior (e.g. a conditional normalizing flow or diffusion model over maps) rather than a point estimate — the state of the art for mass mapping with uncertainty.

Where this can mislead you

Simulation-trained, simulation-limited. The network only knows the physics, noise and systematics that were in its training simulations. If the real universe — or the real instrument — differs (wrong cosmology, baryonic effects, unmodelled systematics), the network can be confidently wrong, and its pretty output hides the problem. This domain shift is the central risk.

Calibration > accuracy. For cosmology the error bars matter more than the mean. A map that looks sharp but whose uncertainties are a factor of two too small will bias your parameters. Networks must be validated on the calibration of their uncertainties against known ground truth — which is precisely the kind of calibration-first benchmarking I do in my own inference work.

MSE smooths peaks. An L2 loss gently blurs the brightest, rarest features — the very peaks that carry the non-Gaussian cosmological signal. Loss design (L1, adversarial, or a peak-aware term) matters, and must be checked against the summary statistics you actually care about, not just RMSE.

None of these is a reason not to use U-Nets — they are a reason to use them like a physicist: with a forward model you trust, uncertainties you have calibrated, and summary statistics that confirm the science survived the network.

7Making it better — and the wider model family

How to improve the exact network trained in §4, and where it sits among the neighbouring model families.

Improving this model

The network in §4 is deliberately minimal (3 levels, 16 channels, MSE loss, 45 epochs on log-normal mocks). The upgrades fall into four groups, roughly in order of scientific payoff:

Architecture

Add capacity and depth (more channels, a fourth downsampling level for a larger receptive field); insert normalisation (Group/Batch-Norm) between conv and ReLU to stabilise training; make the conv blocks residual (ResU-Net) so gradients flow and detail is preserved; add attention gates on the skip connections or a transformer block at the bottleneck (Attention U-Net, TransUNet) for the global context convolutions lack. Replace bilinear upsampling with a learned sub-pixel layer (watching for checkerboard artefacts).

Loss & data — the most important fix for cosmology

MSE is the weakest part: it smooths exactly the peaks that carry the signal. Switch to L1 / Charbonnier, and add a term that penalises mismatch in the summary statistics you care about — power spectrum, peak counts, or a higher-order statistic (bispectrum / skew-spectrum). That trains the network to preserve precisely the non-Gaussian information my own estimators are built to measure. Then: free augmentation from the field's statistical isotropy (rotations / flips), training across a range of noise levels and cosmologies so it does not overfit one survey depth or one universe, and feeding the per-pixel noise / mask level as an extra input channel so it copes with the uneven galaxy distribution and survey holes. Replacing log-normal mocks with ray-traced N-body κ is the honest step up in realism.

Uncertainty — make it probabilistic

A point estimate is not science. Cheap: MC-dropout or a deep ensemble. Proper: make it generative — a conditional normalizing flow or, better, a diffusion / score-based model over maps that samples many plausible κ fields consistent with the data, giving calibrated error bars. This is the current state of the art for mass mapping.

Physics-informed

Fold the known Kaiser–Squires operator into the architecture instead of making the net relearn it — unrolled optimisation, learned-Wiener + net hybrids, or plug-and-play priors ("model-based deep learning"). This respects the physics and extrapolates far better off the training distribution, which is the main failure mode from §6.

How it connects to other AI models

The U-Net is not an island — it is the hub of a family, and several of the improvements above are moves toward a neighbouring model. The map:

Ancestors — where it came from.

Autoencoder
an encoder–decoder trained to reconstruct its own input through a bottleneck. A U-Net is an autoencoder with two changes: skip connections, and supervision against a target (clean κ) rather than the input. Remove the skips and the supervision and you are back to a plain autoencoder.
Fully-Convolutional Network (FCN)
the first network to do dense, per-pixel prediction with convolutions only. The U-Net is a direct refinement of it — FCN upsampled crudely; U-Net added the symmetric decoder and the skip connections that made the output sharp.
CNN classifier (ResNet, VGG)
a standard image classifier is exactly the U-Net's encoder half — convolutions and pooling that shrink an image to a compact summary. The U-Net reuses that contracting path and adds an expanding path to turn the summary back into a map.

Variants — a modified U-Net.

VAE
replace the deterministic bottleneck with a probabilistic latent variable and you have a variational autoencoder — a generative model that can sample new fields. The same encoder–decoder skeleton, now producing a distribution rather than a point.
ResU-Net
put residual connections (the ResNet idea) inside each U-Net block. Easier to train deep, better detail — the merger of the two skip-connection lineages.
Transformer / ViT (TransUNet, Swin-UNet)
graft attention onto the U-Net — typically a transformer block at the bottleneck, or attention gates on the skips. Attention gives the global receptive field convolutions lack; it is the same mechanism as in large language models, applied to image patches instead of word tokens.

Generative backbones — the U-Net is their engine.

GAN (pix2pix)
in image-to-image GANs the generator is a U-Net, trained against a discriminator that judges realism. This adversarial pressure produces sharp, realistic textures — used in cosmology for super-resolution and baryon painting.
Diffusion / score-based models
the deepest modern link: the denoiser inside a diffusion model is almost always a U-Net (plus a time embedding and attention). Diffusion is essentially iterative U-Net denoising; it powers Stable Diffusion and DALL·E, and is now the leading route to calibrated generative mass maps and field emulation.

Neighbours — alternatives and partners.

Neural operators (FNO, DeepONet)
the main alternative for field-to-field problems. The Fourier Neural Operator learns the mapping in Fourier space — a natural contrast to a U-Net for lensing, where the forward operator is already a Fourier multiplier. (There is an FNO comparison in my CFD note.)
Normalizing flows + SBI
not U-Nets, but the usual partner: a U-Net/CNN compresses the map into a summary, and a normalizing flow turns that summary into a posterior on — the field-level inference chain of §5.
Graph / point-cloud nets
for data that do not live on a grid — galaxy catalogues, simulation particles — a graph neural network replaces the grid-based U-Net.
PINN (physics-informed NN)
bakes a PDE or physical constraint into the loss. Not a reconstruction network, but the complement: it enforces physics where the U-Net learns from data, and the two are increasingly combined (the "physics-informed" upgrade above).

8Takeaways

•  A U-Net is an encoder–decoder with skip connections: context on the way down, localisation on the way up, fine detail copied across. That is the whole idea.

•  Change the last layer and loss and it goes from segmentation to regression — which is how it enters physics.

•  On the canonical cosmological inverse problem — weak-lensing mass mapping — a tiny U-Net trained here beats the optimal linear filter, and the same network stripped of its skip connections, because the field is non-Gaussian.

•  The same architecture runs across the Euclid / LSST pipeline: denoising, super-resolution, deblending, field-level inference with SBI.

•  Treat the output as a measurement: get uncertainties, check their calibration, and confirm the non-Gaussian signal survived.

9Terminology

Every term used above, in one place — the deep-learning half and the cosmology half.

The deep-learning terms

Convolution
a small sliding filter applied across an image; the basic operation of a CNN. The same filter weights are reused everywhere, so the network learns local patterns (edges, blobs) with very few parameters.
CNN
convolutional neural network — a network built mostly from convolutions. A U-Net is a particular CNN architecture.
ReLU
"rectified linear unit", the function . The standard nonlinearity between convolutions; without a nonlinearity, stacking layers would collapse to a single linear map.
Pooling / downsampling
shrinking the image (e.g. taking the max of each block). Loses fine location but lets each later unit "see" a bigger region cheaply.
Upsampling
the reverse — growing a small feature map back toward full resolution, in the decoder.
Receptive field
how much of the input a single output unit depends on. Pooling grows it quickly; a large receptive field is what gives "context".
Encoder / decoder
the contracting (down) and expanding (up) halves of the U-Net. The encoder builds an abstract summary; the decoder turns it back into a full-resolution output.
Bottleneck
the lowest-resolution layer in the middle, where the representation is most abstract and most compressed.
Skip connection
a direct link that copies full-resolution encoder features across to the matching decoder level, so fine detail does not have to survive the bottleneck.
Dense prediction
producing an output value for every pixel (a whole map), as opposed to one label for the whole image.
Segmentation
dense prediction where each pixel gets a class (cell/background, void/filament). The U-Net's original task.
Regression
dense prediction where each pixel gets a continuous number (a physical field). What most cosmology uses need.
Loss function
the quantity minimised during training. MSE (mean squared error, "L2") penalises squared differences and tends to smooth; L1 penalises absolute differences and preserves sharp features better.
Training / validation
the network learns on the training set; performance is measured on a held-out validation set it never trained on, to detect overfitting.
RMSE
root-mean-square error — the typical size of the pixel-by-pixel difference between a reconstruction and the truth. Lower is better; the headline number in §4.
MC-dropout / ensemble
two cheap ways to get uncertainty from a network: run it many times with random units switched off, or train several copies, and use the spread.
Super-resolution
predicting a high-resolution output from a low-resolution input.
Inpainting
filling in missing or masked regions of an image from the surrounding context.
Domain shift
when the real data differ from the training simulations, so a network trained on one distribution is applied to another — the main failure mode here.
Calibration
whether the network's stated uncertainties are the right size: do its "1σ" error bars actually contain the truth 68% of the time?

The cosmology terms

Weak lensing
the slight, coherent distortion of distant galaxy shapes by the gravity of intervening matter — a direct probe of the (mostly dark) matter distribution.
Shear
the measurable part of weak lensing: the small stretching of each galaxy's apparent shape. What a survey actually records.
Convergence
the projected total matter density along the line of sight — the "mass map" we want. Shear and convergence are two views of the same lensing field.
Mass mapping
reconstructing the convergence (the mass) from the measured shear . The worked example in §4.
Kaiser–Squires (KS)
the classic, direct inversion from shear to convergence — exact in principle, but it passes the noise straight through.
Shape noise
the dominant noise in weak lensing: galaxies have large intrinsic ellipticities, so each one is a very noisy measurement of the shear.
Power spectrum
how much fluctuation a field has at each scale — its complete two-point description. Two fields can share a power spectrum yet look utterly different (see Gaussian vs. log-normal).
Gaussian random field
a field whose statistics are fully captured by its power spectrum; symmetric, no special peaks. The early universe is very nearly one.
Non-Gaussianity
any departure from Gaussian statistics — skewness, peaks, higher-order correlations — produced by nonlinear gravitational growth. Where the extra cosmological information (and the U-Net's advantage) lives.
Log-normal field
the standard analytic model for the convergence field: a Gaussian field run through , giving realistic skewness and peaks (§4).
Wiener filter
the optimal linear way to denoise a field, weighting each scale by its signal-to-noise. Optimal only if the field is Gaussian — which is why a nonlinear U-Net can beat it.
Bispectrum / skew-spectrum
higher-order statistics that measure non-Gaussianity (three-point correlations and their compressions) — the classical route to the same extra information a U-Net exploits.
CMB
the cosmic microwave background, the oldest light in the universe. "Component separation" unmixes it from Galactic foregrounds; "delensing" undoes the blurring that later matter imposes on it.
-modes
a curl-like pattern in the CMB polarisation; a primordial -mode signal would be evidence for inflation, which is why delensing to reveal it matters.
Cosmic web
the large-scale structure of matter: voids, walls, filaments and nodes.
N-body / hydro simulation
simulations of structure formation. N-body follows gravity only (cheap); hydrodynamic runs add gas and stars (expensive) — hence "baryon painting".
Sunyaev–Zel'dovich (SZ)
a distortion of the CMB by hot gas in galaxy clusters; a way to detect clusters.
Simulation-based inference (SBI)
estimating cosmological parameters by comparing data to simulations, without writing down an explicit likelihood — often paired with a U-Net that compresses the map first.
Normalizing flow
a flexible neural model of a probability distribution; a common SBI tool for turning a learned summary into a posterior on parameters.
Euclid / LSST
the current "Stage-IV" surveys: ESA's Euclid satellite and the Vera Rubin Observatory's LSST, imaging billions of galaxies — the scale at which fast learned methods become necessary.

Reproducibility. Every figure and number in this note comes from a single self-contained script: it draws the architecture schematic, simulates the log-normal convergence fields, applies the Kaiser–Squires forward/inverse operator with shape noise, fits an empirical Wiener filter and a tuned wavelet denoiser as fair baselines, and trains both the skip-free CNN and the full U-Net above (PyTorch, 45 epochs, CPU). Reported errors are RMSE against the true field on 200 held-out validation maps: noisy KS 0.636, KS+smoothing 0.480, Wiener 0.435, sparse/wavelet 0.523, CNN (no skips) 0.555, U-Net 0.376.
